summary: Mike Padlipsky replies to RFC 514 and RFC 519, which disagree about network information: one finds too many requests for it, the other says newcomers find it hard to learn about hosts. He tries to resolve the feast-or-famine puzzle. It is a commentary.

eli5.summary: Some people had too many questions to answer and others could not find answers. This author tries to explain how both can be true.

questions: what is the arpanet resource notebook
subtitle: Too much information is asked for, yet newcomers cannot find any. The Resource Notebook is the answer.

tldr.problem: RFC 514 complains of too many requests for host information, while RFC 519 says newcomers find it hard to learn about hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Mike Padlipsky argues both problems share one answer: the Network Resource Notebook, which already lists technical liaisons, host information and references, should be treated as the primary source of host information.
tldr.outcome: It is a commentary. He admits the Notebook needs stronger content and wider dissemination, and is not meant to replace individual hosts' user manuals.

today: The unit metadata lists this RFC's status as Unknown and records no replacement. It responds to RFC 514 and RFC 519.

sections.title: Feast and Famine
sections.content:
Padlipsky notes that RFC 514 returns to the theme of RFC 459: too many people ask for too much information about network hosts. RFC 519 returns to the theme of RFC 369: it is not easy to learn to use hosts. The network seems to have both a feast and a famine of information, and he sets out to resolve the apparent contradiction.

For big servers, he says, the burden is worse. Multics alone has something like 50 cubic feet of system listings.
sections.eli5: Some people get buried in requests while others cannot find help. He wants to show how both can be true.

sections.title: The Unread Resource Notebook
sections.content:
Padlipsky says the information exists but is not used. As Network Technical Liaison for Multics he never heard from the UCSB investigators, and he saw many botched login attempts in the error logs. The Resource Notebook lists technical liaisons, gives information about hosts, and points to other published information. Its Multics section offers a Multics Programmers Manual to any network site on request.

In his view the Notebook would have solved the UCSB group's problems, and would have steered the RML requests to people who could explain why they were inappropriate.
sections.eli5: The guidebook already tells newcomers who to call and how to log in, but they did not open it.

sections.title: What the Notebook Is and Is Not
sections.content: He does not call the Notebook a panacea. It needs stronger content and wide dissemination, perhaps through the planned Network New Users' Packet or on microfiche. It does not replace individual hosts' users' manuals, but is a partial repository for documentation of generic commands. He asks the NWG to agree to view it as the "primary source of Host information".
sections.eli5: The guidebook is not perfect, but it is the best place to start, so use it and make it better.
